Home Server, Public Address

Vishnu Vardhan · 11 October 2026

A web application running on a personal computer at home can be reached from anywhere on the internet, without opening any port on the home router. This article explains why the default network setup blocks such access, why the usual fix of port forwarding was not used, and how a Cloudflare Tunnel provides a public address by letting the computer make the first connection. It also covers the setup steps and every error encountered along the way.

Why a home computer cannot be reached

A personal computer on a home network does not have a public address. The internet service provider assigns one public address to the household, and the router shares it among every device. Each device receives a private address, such as 192.168.1.20, which has meaning only inside the house. This arrangement is called network address translation, or NAT.

NAT works in one direction. When the computer requests a web page, the router records the request and forwards the reply to the correct device. When a request arrives from the internet without a matching record, the router discards it. A server running on the personal computer is therefore unreachable from outside the network, even though it is running and listening for connections.

This behaviour protects the home network from casual scanning. It also blocks the visitors the application is meant to serve. Any approach to publishing the application must work with this boundary, not around it.

Port forwarding and why it was not used

The conventional method of allowing inbound access is port forwarding. The router is configured to pass traffic arriving on a chosen port, such as 443, to the personal computer. Port forwarding works and has been used for many years. It was not chosen for this project, for four reasons.

  • The computer becomes directly exposed. Its service listens on the public internet, where automated scanners will find it. Any weakness in the application or the operating system becomes reachable by anyone.
  • Encryption and naming require ongoing work. Browsers expect encrypted connections, which means a certificate issued for a name and renewed on schedule. Residential public addresses can also change, so the name must be updated when they do.
  • The router boundary is altered. The router is the protection for every device in the house. Each forwarding rule is an exception to that protection, and an error in any rule affects the whole network.
  • Provider policies can prevent it. Some providers block inbound traffic on common ports, and some place customers behind shared addresses, where forwarding cannot work.

Why GitHub Pages was not used

Before settling on a tunnel, three designs were considered. The first was to host the React page on GitHub Pages and tunnel only the API. That design places the page and the API on different origins, so it requires CORS configuration and a build-time API address. The second was to tunnel the page and the API through two separate routes. The third was to serve the built page from Spring. The chosen design uses one hostname for the page, with Vite forwarding /api to Spring. It keeps both parts on the personal computer, avoids CORS, and needs only one route for the chat.

How a tunnel reverses the connection

A Cloudflare Tunnel changes the direction in which the first connection is made. The personal computer opens the connection outward to Cloudflare, and visitor requests travel back along that connection. No inbound port needs to be opened.

A small program, cloudflared, runs on the personal computer. It establishes an encrypted session with Cloudflare. Outbound connections are permitted by default on a home network, and the router already tracks them, so the router configuration does not change. Once the session is open, Cloudflare can send requests down it.

Every packet on that session belongs to a connection initiated by the personal computer. The router treats it like any other outgoing traffic and passes the replies back in the usual way. Nothing unsolicited arrives at the network boundary, so there is nothing for the router to discard and no opening for an attacker to use.

Three systems are involved

The setup depends on three systems, and each one has a specific role. Knowing which one is responsible for which behaviour makes failures easier to locate.

SystemRoleWhat it had to allow or do
CloudflarePublic entry point. The edge accepts visitor connections in several data centres; the dashboard reported Dallas locations for this connectorTerminate HTTPS, match the hostname to a route, and deliver requests down the open session
WindowsRuns cloudflared as a service that registers with the Service Control Manager and survives rebootsPermit the outbound session through Windows Defender Firewall, and allow the service to be installed with administrator rights
Home router (Spectrum)Performs NAT and tracks outgoing sessionsNothing was changed. Outbound sessions are tracked by default, and no port was forwarded

The router needed no configuration. The firewall needed no new rule for the connector to run, because the connector only makes outbound connections. The Vite preview server is bound to 127.0.0.1. The Spring server is listening on all interfaces at present, so restricting it to 127.0.0.1 is listed as an open item.

What the connection is

The outbound session is built in layers. Each layer has a separate job, and understanding the layers makes the security properties easier to see. The diagram below shows the sequence as it happens when the connector starts.

Three layers stack on one another. The transport moves bytes between the two addresses. TLS or QUIC encrypts the traffic, so no device on the path can read or alter it. The tunnel protocol then carries many separate requests across the single session. This last point explains why one connection is enough for an entire site.

The connector also establishes several connections to different Cloudflare data centres, which provides redundancy. The following diagram shows that step and the moment the tunnel is marked as having a connector.

Hostnames and DNS

When a public hostname is added to a tunnel, Cloudflare creates a DNS record that points the name to the tunnel. The name does not resolve to the home network. It resolves to Cloudflare's own addresses. The association between the hostname and the tunnel is stored in Cloudflare's configuration.

One request, from start to finish

The steps for a single request are straightforward. The visitor's browser resolves the hostname to Cloudflare, which terminates the encrypted connection. Cloudflare reads the hostname, finds the tunnel mapped to it, and sends the request down the open session. The connector on the personal computer delivers the request to the local service. The response returns along the same path.

Figure 4 shows the same path for this application. Loading the page and sending a chat message use the same hostname. The difference is the final hop. A page load ends at the preview server, and a chat message continues to the API.

A tunnel status of Healthy means that the session between the personal computer and Cloudflare is open. It does not mean that the application is listening. Two conditions must both hold. The tunnel must be connected, and a service must be accepting connections on the local address the route targets. If the first condition holds and the second does not, the visitor receives an error from Cloudflare, even though the tunnel is working.

Loading the page follows the top row. The browser requests the hostname, Cloudflare matches the route, and cloudflared hands the request to the Vite preview server on port 4173. Vite returns the compiled page. Sending a chat message follows the bottom row. The page calls a relative address beginning with /api, which stays on the same hostname. Vite forwards those calls to Spring on port 8090. The browser never needs to know that Spring exists.

Why one hostname serves both the page and the API

Browsers prevent a page from calling a server with a different origin, unless that server explicitly permits it through a mechanism called Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, or CORS. Configuring CORS is possible, but it requires matching rules on both sides, and an error in either one produces failures that are difficult to diagnose.

Serving the page and the API from one hostname removes the requirement. The page and the API share an origin, so the browser does not perform the cross-origin check. Vite handles the forwarding, and Spring needs no special configuration for the public site.

Components on the personal computer

ComponentPortFunctionReachable through the tunnel
Vite preview server4173Serves the compiled React page and forwards /api requests to SpringYes, this is the route target
Spring Boot API8090Application server that searches closed tickets and ranks matchesOnly through the Vite forwarding rule
Ollama11434Local language modelNo. It has no authentication and is never routed
cloudflaredNot applicableMaintains the outbound session to Cloudflare, installed as a Windows serviceNot applicable

Ollama is deliberately excluded from the tunnel. It does not require a login, and it listens only on the local machine by default. Routing it through a public hostname would give every visitor direct use of the model.

Setup procedure

Each step below addresses a specific requirement. The screenshots show the state of the configuration at that point.

  1. Assign a fixed port to the API. Spring Boot defaults to 8080, which other Spring projects on the same computer already use. Two services on one port would cause a route to deliver requests to the wrong application without any error. In application.yaml, the setting is server.port: 8090.
  2. Configure the frontend server. The React application is compiled and served by Vite's preview command, which defaults to port 4173. The configuration file below sets the host, the port, and a strict port check. It also forwards /api to Spring.
  3. Allow the public hostname. Vite refuses requests whose host name is not on its allowed list. This protects against DNS rebinding attacks. Without the entry, the public address returns a 403 response. The hostname is added to preview.allowedHosts, as shown above.
  4. Build and verify locally. Run npm run build to compile the application, then npm run preview to serve it. Open 127.0.0.1:4173 and send a chat message. The screenshot below shows the build output and the local preview, with the chat answering from the local server. Local verification must succeed before the tunnel is involved.
  5. Confirm that Spring is listening. In PowerShell, run Test-NetConnection 127.0.0.1 -Port 8090. The result should show TcpTestSucceeded : True. Command Prompt does not include this command.
  6. Install the connector. In the Cloudflare dashboard, create a tunnel. The dashboard displays Windows instructions with an installation command. The installer is a Windows package, and Windows blocks downloaded packages until they are unblocked in the file's Properties. The service registration requires an elevated Command Prompt. The screenshots below show the dashboard instructions, with the token removed.
  7. Verify the connector. After the service is installed, the tunnel should show as Healthy. A Healthy tunnel with no routes serves nothing, so the next step adds a route.
  8. Add a published application route. Choose Published application, set the subdomain to kanbanassist, the domain to vishnuvardhan.io, and the service to 127.0.0.1:4173. The screenshots show the route dialog and the overview after the route is saved. The example in the third image uses port 8080 and is included only to illustrate the field layout.
  9. Test from outside the network. Open the public address in a browser that is not connected to the home network, and send a chat message. Testing only from inside the house can conceal problems that a visitor would encounter.

Building the frontend

A React application is compiled into static files. The compiled output is a single page, index.html, together with JavaScript and CSS files. The browser loads the page, runs the JavaScript, and calls the API. The files require no Node.js process at runtime, so any web server can host them, including the preview server used here.

The current application uses relative API paths, so the same build works on any host that serves both the page and the API. If the application adds client-side routes, the server configuration must return the page for unrecognised paths. Without that, a visitor who opens a deep link directly receives a 404 response.

Diagnostics: which command answers which question

When a request fails, the question is which hop failed. Each of the following tools answers one question.

Command or toolQuestion it answersWhat to look for
Test-NetConnection 127.0.0.1 -Port 8090Is anything listening on this port?TcpTestSucceeded : True
Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 8090Which process holds the port?The owning process ID, which Get-Process -Id resolves to a name
curl.exe -v http://127.0.0.1:8090/What does the service return?The HTTP status line and headers
nslookup kanbanassist.vishnuvardhan.ioWhere does the name resolve?Cloudflare addresses, not the home network
Cloudflare Live logsAre requests reaching the tunnel, and with what status?Status codes such as 200 and 304 for successful requests

Three status codes in this setup had distinct meanings. A 403 from the public address came from Vite's host check. A 404 from Spring at / is expected, because the API has no root page. A 502 from Cloudflare means the tunnel delivered a request but nothing was listening at the target, which is the state the tunnel was in when the preview server had stopped.

Problems encountered and how each was resolved

The setup did not proceed without difficulty. Some problems resulted from Windows, some from the way the components depend on one another, and some from configuration mistakes. They are recorded below in the order they occurred. Where the cause is not known, the entry says so.

The installer did not start

Double-clicking the downloaded installer produced no result. Windows marks files downloaded from the internet, and some installers will not run until the mark is removed. The fix was the Unblock option in the file's Properties dialog. The command was then run from an elevated prompt.

Access was denied when registering the service

Registering a Windows service requires administrator rights. A standard Command Prompt does not have them. Running the command from an elevated prompt resolved the error. The screenshot below shows the successful result: the Cloudflared service was installed.

The PowerShell command was entered in Command Prompt

The same screenshot records a second error. The command Test-NetConnection was typed into Command Prompt, which does not recognise it. The command exists only in PowerShell. Running it there resolved the error. Command Prompt was still used for curl, which is why the screenshot shows both.

Port 8080 was already in use by other projects

Spring Boot's default port is 8080, and other Spring projects on the same computer use it. Two services on one port would route requests to the wrong application without an error. The API was set to 8090. The startup log confirmed the change: Tomcat started on port 8090 (http).

A route pointed to a port with no listener

An early frontend route targeted port 3000, which belongs to no part of the project. Visitors would have reached a port where nothing was listening. The route was changed to 4173, and strictPort was set in the Vite configuration.

The preview server had stopped, and the port check failed

Test-NetConnection 127.0.0.1 -Port 4173 returned TcpTestSucceeded : False, with PingSucceeded : True. The ping confirms that the computer responds. The failed TCP test confirms that nothing was listening on the port. The preview server had stopped. Restarting npm run preview resolved the problem, and the port check against 8090 then succeeded.

The browser reported a refused connection

The browser displayed ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED for port 4173, and curl reported the same condition. The cause was the same as in the previous problem. A refused connection means that the port is closed. It does not indicate an error in the route. The fix was to restart the preview server.

Testing on the wrong port

For a period, testing was performed on localhost:5173, which is the development server started with npm run dev. That server reloads on every change and is useful during development. The public route targets the preview server on port 4173, which serves the compiled build. The two servers can behave differently. From that point, all testing used port 4173, because that is the port the tunnel reaches.

The chat did not respond on the preview server

The preview server delivered the page, but chat requests did not reach Spring. The initial explanation was a missing proxy rule in the preview block. That explanation was incorrect. Vite's documentation states that the preview server uses the server.proxy rules when no preview.proxy is defined, so the forwarding rule already applied. The necessary change was an explicit host, port and strictPort setting, which keeps the preview server behaviour consistent.

The public address returned 403

With the route active, the public address returned a 403 response with the message "Blocked request. This host ("kanbanassist.vishnuvardhan.io") is not allowed." The message came from Vite, not from Cloudflare or Spring. Vite refuses host names that are not on its allowed list. The message also named the setting to change, preview.allowedHosts. After the hostname was added and the preview server restarted, the page loaded.

The tunnel name was required

The Create a Tunnel form does not proceed without a name. The name kanbanassist was entered. The name is also used by the connector installed as a Windows service, so it should be chosen with that in mind.

A healthy tunnel with no routes serves nothing

After the connector was installed, the dashboard showed the tunnel as Healthy with one replica and zero routes. That status confirms the connection to Cloudflare. It does not direct any traffic. The route is the second part of the configuration, and it is required before the application is reachable.

The route lists https:// for plain HTTP servers

The Routes table lists both services with https://127.0.0.1 addresses. The local servers use plain HTTP, and the public site works with the current setting, so the configuration was left unchanged. This item is open. The setting used for the final hop to the personal computer needs to be confirmed. The table also shows a second route, for api.kanbanassist.vishnuvardhan.io, which targets port 8090. The chat path does not require that route, because the page calls /api on its own hostname.

An unexplained TLS handshake in the Spring log

Spring logged the following warning during testing:

Error parsing HTTP request header
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Invalid character found in method name
[0x16 0x03 0x01 0x05 0xd8 ...]. HTTP method names must be tokens

The bytes 0x16 0x03 0x01 begin a TLS handshake, which is the first message of an encrypted connection. Spring listens with plain HTTP and cannot interpret those bytes as a request. An earlier explanation attributed the event to the route's HTTPS setting. That explanation is not sufficient, because the public site functions with the same setting. The source has not been identified. It may be an internet scanner or a client on the personal computer. The item remains open.

A 404 response at the root path

Spring returns a 404 for the root path. This is expected, because the API has no page at /. The meaningful test is a request to a path under /api, sent through the preview server. A visitor who requests the root of the API hostname receives the same 404 unless a route is defined for that path.

The bundle size warning

The production build completed, and Vite reported that some chunks exceed 500 kB. The main JavaScript file is about 1.1 MB. The warning does not block the build. Code splitting is the appropriate remedy when load time becomes significant. It has not been implemented.

The public test was run before local verification

An early recommendation was to test the public address before the local checks had passed. That order was incorrect. The sequence that isolates failures is local verification first, then the tunnel, then a device outside the home network. Each stage narrows the possible causes of a failure.

Trade-offs

A tunnel makes a personal computer reachable. It does not convert the computer into a production server, and it does not eliminate every risk. The following points describe the current arrangement.

  • The token is a password. The install command contains a token that authorises the connector to run the tunnel under the account. Anyone who obtains it can run a tunnel as that account. It should never be pasted into a chat or published. If it is exposed, the dashboard's Refresh token action invalidates it, and the connector must be reinstalled with the new command.
  • The router configuration is unchanged. The firewall and settings of the home router remain as they were. No inbound port is opened.
  • A public address is not required. The personal computer does not need its own address, and changes to the residential address do not affect the connection, because the session is initiated from inside the network.
  • Traffic is encrypted to the edge. The visitor's connection is encrypted up to Cloudflare, and the tunnel carries the traffic onward over its own encrypted session. Cloudflare can read the traffic at the edge, so this arrangement involves the same trust as any hosted service.
  • Access is not restricted. Anyone with the link can use the chat. Cloudflare Access can require an email-based sign-in in front of the hostname. It has not been configured.
  • Availability depends on the personal computer. If the computer sleeps or loses its connection, the application is unavailable. A cloud host avoids this, but it also moves the model and the data off the personal computer.
  • The preview server is intended for development-scale use. It provides a stable way to serve a compiled page from one machine. A production web server or a managed host is more appropriate for substantial traffic.
  • The language model remains private. Ollama has no authentication and is not routed through the tunnel.
  • The production bundle is large. The JavaScript file is about 1.1 MB. Vite reports a warning above 500 kB. The warning is advisory, and code splitting is the remedy when it matters.
Open items. Access control has not been configured. The Spring server has not been restricted to 127.0.0.1, which would limit it to the local proxy. The source of the TLS handshake in the log has not been identified. The service type of the route requires confirmation. Each item will be resolved and this article updated accordingly.

Next steps

The most important next step is Cloudflare Access, which replaces an open link with an authenticated sign-in. After that, the Spring server should be bound to 127.0.0.1 so that only the local proxy can reach it. The route's service type should be confirmed, and the TLS source should be identified by listing the processes that hold connections on port 8090.

The underlying principle is that a server behind a closed network can still be reached, provided the connection is initiated from inside. The tunnel is a single program on a single machine, with one outbound connection. Every public address is a route that can be inspected and removed.
